title: Even and Odd Functions and Their Symmetry
author: Muhammad Abdullah Athar
problemStatement: Define even and odd functions, give one example of each, and describe the symmetry each type forces on the graph.
finalAnswer: $f$ is even when $f(-x) = f(x)$ (mirror symmetry about the $y$-axis, e.g. $x^2$); $f$ is odd when $f(-x) = -f(x)$ (rotational symmetry about the origin, e.g. $x^3$).

steps.title: State the Algebraic Tests
steps.mathExpression: \text{even: } f(-x) = f(x), \qquad \text{odd: } f(-x) = -f(x) \ \text{for all } x \in D
steps.explanation: Both definitions require the domain itself to be symmetric about 0 (if x is allowed, so is -x) and the identity to hold everywhere in the domain, not just at a few points.
steps.why: The identities in x are the only rigorous way to certify parity of a function.

steps.title: Read the Geometry
steps.mathExpression: f(-x) = f(x) \iff y\text{-axis mirror}; \quad f(-x) = -f(x) \iff \text{origin rotation}
steps.explanation: For an even function, the point (x, y) on the graph brings (-x, y) along as its mirror image across the y-axis. For an odd function, (x, y) forces (-x, -y), which is the 180-degree rotation of the point about the origin.
steps.why: Pairing each algebraic identity with its picture is exactly what the review question asks for.

steps.title: Verify with Examples
steps.explanation: The parabola y = x^2 is even; sin x and x^3 are odd. Most functions are neither: x^2 + x fails both tests, since -(f(x)) and f(-x) disagree with f(x).
steps.why: Checking concrete formulas locks in the definitions and warns that neither is the default case.
